2. Main points
Vacancy estimates decreased on the quarter, with early estimates for July to September 2026 suggesting a decrease of 21,000 (2.9%) vacancies to 691,000, compared with April to June 2026; this is the first time the total has been below 700,000 since February to April 2021.
Vacancy estimates decreased in 14 of the 18 industry sectors, compared with April to June 2026; the largest industry decrease was in construction (down 7,000 vacancies).
Vacancy estimates decreased in 4 of the 5 employment size bands, compared with April to June 2026; the largest decrease was for businesses with 1 to 9 employees (down 21,000 vacancies).
There were 2.4 unemployed people per vacancy in June to August 2026, down from 2.5 in March to May 2026, a level at which the ratio has remained since July to September 2025.
The UK vacancy rate (the proportion of unfilled jobs to total jobs in the economy) was 2.1% in July to September 2026, down 0.1 percentage points since April to June 2026.

3. Vacancies for July to September 2026
Figure 1: The estimated number of vacancies has seen a quarterly decrease of 21,000 to 691,000

Source: Vacancy Survey from the Office for National Statistics

 Image

The early estimate of the number of vacancies in the UK decreased by 21,000 (2.9%) to 691,000 in July to September 2026, compared with April to June 2026. This is the largest quarterly fall since January to March 2026, which was also a fall of 21,000 vacancies. This change remains within our confidence interval for estimates of approximately plus or minus 32,000 vacancies (read more in Section 7: Data sources and quality).
On the year, vacancies decreased by 37,000 (5.1%). The last time the estimated number of vacancies was 691,000 or fewer was in February to April 2021, when there were 660,000 vacancies. Outside of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic period, the last time there were 691,000 or fewer vacancies was in July to September 2014, when there were 686,000 vacancies.
The headline vacancy estimates are based on three-month averages, which naturally involve some time lag. We provide insights into trends in September 2026 in our X06: Single month vacancies estimates dataset (read more in Section 7: Data sources and quality). We advise caution when comparing data sources, because the single month data are not seasonally adjusted.
We provide further insights in our Labour demand volumes by Standard Occupation Classification (SOC 2020), UK dataset, which includes official statistics in development sourced from Textkernel data. We will update these estimates regularly as part of our Economic activity and social change in the UK, real-time indicators bulletins. We advise caution when using these alternative data sources because the data are not seasonally adjusted or directly comparable.
The unemployment-to-vacancy ratio is a measure of labour market "tightness", meaning that it shows how many unemployed people there are for each available unfilled job. An increase in the unemployment-to-vacancy ratio implies that the labour market is less tight, as there are more available workers to fill those vacant jobs.
There were 2.4 unemployed people per vacancy in June to August 2026. This is down from 2.5 in March to May 2026, a level at which the ratio has remained since July to September 2025. The ratio was also 2.4 in the same period a year ago.
Another indicator of labour demand is the vacancy rate, also referred to as the job openings rate. The rate captures the number of unfilled jobs (or vacancies) that an employer is actively recruiting workers to fill, as a proportion of the total number of jobs (including filled and unfilled jobs) in the economy. An increase in the vacancy rate implies a higher demand for workers in roles that are currently not filled.
The UK vacancy rate was 2.1% in July to September 2026, down 0.1 percentage points both on the quarter and on the year.

The estimated total number of vacancies decreased by 21,000 (2.9%) in July to September 2026, compared with April to June 2026, falling in 14 of the 18 industry sectors. The industry with the largest percentage decrease in vacancies was construction, which was down 20.5%. This industry also had the largest volume decrease of 7,000 vacancies. This was followed by other service activities, which was down 19.9% (3,000 vacancies).
Total vacancies decreased by 37,000 (5.1%) in July to September 2026, compared with the same period a year ago. There were declines in 13 of the 18 industry sectors. The industry with the largest annual percentage decrease in vacancies was water supply, sewerage, waste and remediation activities, down 23.0% (2,000 vacancies). Professional scientific and technical activities had the largest annual volume decrease of 9,000 vacancies (11.6%). This was followed by education, which was down 7,000 vacancies (13.3%).
The industry with the highest demand for workers was mining and quarrying, with a vacancy rate of 3.3% in July to September 2026. This was followed by financial and insurance activities, which has a vacancy rate of 2.9%. The industries with the lowest demand for workers were the arts, entertainment and recreation sector, and education, with vacancy rates of 1.4% and 1.5%, respectively.

Of the five employment size bands, four saw decreases in the number of vacancies on the quarter to July to September 2026. The largest quarterly decrease was in businesses with 1 to 9 employees, down 21,000 (21.1%) to 77,000 vacancies. Outside of the pandemic, this is the lowest level for this employment size band since June to August 2013, when there were 77,000 vacancies.
The only employment size band with an increase on the quarter was businesses with 250 to 2,499 employees, up 2,000 (1.2%) vacancies. All other size bands were down 1,000 vacancies.
The number of vacancies decreased over the year in the three smallest employment size bands. The largest decrease was for businesses with 1 to 9 employees, down 38,000 (32.8%) vacancies.
Feedback from our Vacancy Survey continues to suggest that smaller firms may not be recruiting because of increases in labour costs.

4. Jobs for June 2026
Before publishing our Vacancies and jobs in the UK June bulletin, we undertook additional analysis on our headline workforce jobs series as part of our quality assurance processes. Our analysis indicated mixed and emerging evidence of evolving seasonal patterns in both our headline employee jobs and self-employment jobs series. These seasonal patterns are more evident in self-employment jobs. More information can be found in Section 7: Data sources and quality.
Workforce jobs (WFJ) estimates are provided by various sources, and our latest estimates for June 2026 were published in September 2026. Estimates of employee jobs in the private sector are from business surveys with a reference date of 12 June 2026. Estimates of self-employment jobs are drawn from our Labour Force Survey (LFS), which covers a three-month period from the start of May 2026 to the end of July 2026.
Early estimates suggest there were 36.7 million WFJ in the UK in June 2026. This is an annual increase of 60,000 (0.2%) from the level of a year ago; this was caused by an increase of 46,000 (0.1%) in the employee jobs component, and an increase in the number of government-supported trainees, which was up 23,000 (66.2%). However, there was a decrease of 10,000 (0.2%) in the self-employment jobs component, and the number of HM Forces jobs was slightly up by 2,000 jobs (1.2%) on the year.
